result:
The word "window" comes from Old Norse *vindauga*: wind-eye. Before glass, a window was a hole in the wall or roof where smoke left and weather came in, and someone looked at that hole and saw an eye for the wind. I think about this more than is reasonable.

Emerson called language fossil poetry, and he was right. Most ordinary words began as somebody's metaphor, a small act of imagination that worked so well everyone forgot it was one. A "daisy" is the day's eye, because it opens at dawn and closes at dusk. "Muscle" comes from the Latin for little mouse, since a flexing bicep apparently looked like a mouse moving under the skin. "Disaster" means a bad star. A "companion" is a person you share bread with.

What I like is that nobody planned any of this. There was no committee. Someone said a thing at a fire or a market, the person next to them repeated it, and a thousand years later we use it to complain about drafts. The poems wore smooth like coins, until the image rubbed off and only the value remained.

It makes me suspect we are doing the same thing now, without noticing. We "scroll" through pages that have never been rolled up. We "dial" phones with no dials. Somewhere in today's slang is a phrase that will outlast every building currently standing, its origin a puzzle for some future person who wonders why we said it and looks it up, delighted.
